content.thinking:
I need to draft the postmortem using placeholder names instead of actual figures—things like {A1}, {duration}—avoiding any real digits entirely. I'm starting to trace the chain of causation for why shopper totals didn't reconcile, using evidence labels rather than concrete numbers.

Service health logs stayed normal through the incident, so the issue wasn't an outage—it was that totals got written incorrectly while everything else looked healthy. I'm matching the onset timing to when a flag got switched on, noting a slight discrepancy between two evidence sources but treating the earlier record as authoritative, and I'm careful to describe timing only in relative terms since I can't write actual timestamps. For the root cause, I'm concluding that enabling the monthly-spend-feature flag activated a spend-total computation path that produced wrong totals, though the exact mechanism remains unestablished—a proposed fix exists but hasn't been verified yet, so I'm flagging that as inferred rather than confirmed, and moving on to contributing factors.

I'm noting the detection check only runs periodically, creating a lag—so I need new action items for running checks more frequently and after flag changes, gating flag rollouts behind staged rollout with reconciliation checks, and separately addressing repair of the already-corrupted totals through backfill/recompute, since existing action items don't cover that. I'm assembling these into labeled action items (detect, mitigate, prevent) while avoiding writing raw digits in the prose, and noting the assumptions underlying the causal inference—particularly that the flag's role is inferred from timing correlation alone, with the timestamp discrepancy between sources left unresolved.

For the executive summary and lessons, I'm highlighting what went right—the periodic check caught the issue even without user-visible errors, and Argus pinpointed the flag change quickly, limiting the shortfall—versus what went wrong, namely the detection lag itself.

action_items.item: Run the spend-integrity check much more often, and trigger it automatically after any change to monthly-spend-feature or another flag touching spend totals, so drift is caught within minutes or hours rather than days.
Recompute and repair the shopper totals already written wrongly since the onset, using the purchases as the source of truth, and confirm with the integrity check that none remain unreconciled.
Require flags that change how persistent data is written to roll out in stages, with a reconciliation check on the exposed shoppers before widening.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' stored spend totals did not match their purchases. {A1} of {A2} totals were affected, the widest short by {A3}, and the oldest affected purchase was recorded at {A4}. The fault was still present at the last reading.

The wrong totals were written without any visible operational failure. The logs show only ordinary background noise, such as shoppers disconnecting, and normal page renders. Metrics show no departure around the onset, so nothing signalled the corruption except the integrity check.

The onset coincides with the monthly-spend-feature flag being switched on by an admin just before the first affected purchase. The service logged the flag as on in its evaluations, and no deploy happened in the lookback. The timing, not a demonstrated mechanism, links the flag to the bad totals.

The flag enabled a new spend-total computation path, which appears to write incorrect totals. The evidence stops here: the record does not show what is wrong inside that path. A draft fix has been proposed but is not yet verified.

contributing_factors.factor: The integrity check that compares totals with purchases runs only every {A5} days, so wrong totals can accumulate for that long before anyone is alerted.
A flag that changes how persistent data is written was switched on for everyone with no staged rollout and no reconciliation check afterwards.
Putting the flag back only stops new bad totals. The totals already written stay wrong, and no repair is planned in the record.

Argus could not confirm within its waiting time that putting the flag back worked, because no fast signal exists for total correctness. It therefore only recommended the action, and the rollback waited for a person.

input.executive_summary: Shoppers' stored spend totals have been wrong since {began}. The integrity check found {A1} of {A2} totals not matching the purchases behind them, and the widest was short by {A3}. The service was still broken at the last reading, so the fault lasted at least {duration}. The service stayed fast and showed no unusual errors, so nobody noticed until the check ran, and it runs only every {A5} days. A feature flag for monthly spend had been switched on just before the first bad purchase, and that is the leading suspect. Argus took no action itself because it could not have told whether the fix worked within the time it waits. It recommended that a person put the flag back and proposed a draft code fix. Putting the flag back will stop new bad totals but will not repair the ones already written.

got_lucky: The account pages kept working and nothing visibly failed, so shoppers were not blocked, though their stored totals were wrong.
The flag change was recorded in the change history and its timing matched the first bad purchase, which gave a clear lead; without it the cause would have been hard to find.
went_well: Argus raised the investigation straight away and reached a leading candidate, the flag change, within seconds of the alert.
Argus did not act on a fix it could not verify, and it handed the rollback to a person with a clear recommendation.
A draft pull request for a fix was proposed soon after.
went_wrong: The corruption went undetected for at least {duration} because the only detector runs every {A5} days.
No metric moved, so ordinary monitoring could not see the fault, and there is no pre-onset baseline to compare against.
The rollback has not yet happened, so bad totals may still be accumulating.

input.root_cause: Switching on the monthly-spend-feature flag put a new spend-total computation path into use, and from then on it wrote shopper totals that do not match the purchases behind them. The record does not show what is wrong inside that path, and nothing checked totals against purchases when the flag changed, so the fault went unseen until the periodic integrity check.
